title: Keigo Higashino, Japan's Bestselling Mystery Novelist, Dies at 68
excerpt: The author of 'The Devotion of Suspect X' and the Detective Galileo series died of colon cancer on July 23, leaving behind 106 published works and over 100 million copies sold.
body:
• Keigo Higashino, one of Japan's most prolific and popular mystery writers, died of colon cancer on July 23 at the age of 68.
  • His 106 published works sold over 100 million copies in Japan and were translated into dozens of languages, with nearly 20 adapted into films and TV series.
  • Higashino's signature novel 'The Devotion of Suspect X' won the Naoki Prize and earned nominations at the Edgar Allan Poe Awards in the United States.
  • A final installment in his Detective Galileo series is scheduled for release on August 5, just days after his death.

Keigo Higashino, the Japanese mystery novelist whose intricate plots and psychologically driven crime fiction earned him a readership of hundreds of millions across Asia and beyond, died on July 23 of colon cancer. He was 68.

His publisher Kodansha confirmed the death on July 28, noting that funeral services had already been held privately by his family. "The stories he wrote will undoubtedly continue to captivate countless readers," Kodansha said in a statement.

From Engineer to Literary Giant

Born on February 4, 1958, in the Ikuno-ku ward of Osaka, Higashino grew up in a working-class neighbourhood. He studied electrical engineering at Osaka Prefecture University, where he also captained the archery club — a detail that would later inform his fiction. After graduating, he worked as an engineer at Nippon Denso (now DENSO), writing novels in the evenings and on weekends.

His persistence paid off in 1985, when his debut novel Hōkago (After School) won the prestigious Edogawa Rampo Prize for unpublished mystery fiction. He left engineering the following year to write full-time in Tokyo.

A Career Built on Reinvention

Higashino's breakthrough was gradual but decisive. In 1998, Himitsu (later published in English as Naoko) won the Mystery Writers of Japan Award and was adapted into a feature film. But it was The Devotion of Suspect X in 2006 that cemented his reputation internationally. The novel won the Naoki Prize after five prior nominations and the Honkaku Mystery Award, and was ranked the top mystery novel of the year in Japan.

"The stories he wrote will undoubtedly continue to captivate countless readers."

— Kodansha, publisher statement

The English translation earned nominations for both the Edgar Award and the Barry Award in the United States, while Newcomer was later shortlisted for the British Crime Writers' Association's Dagger awards. The Devotion of Suspect X became something of a signature work, inverting the traditional whodunit by revealing the killer's identity early and instead exploring the emotional weight of loyalty and guilt.

Higashino wrote across two major detective series — Detective Galileo, featuring physicist Manabu Yukawa, and the Police Detective Kaga series — alongside dozens of standalone novels, short story collections, essays, and even a children's picture book. The Galileo series, adapted into television dramas and films starring Masaharu Fukuyama, sold over 10 million copies alone.

Massive Popularity Across Asia

While Higashino was ubiquitous in Japanese bookshops, his influence extended far beyond his home country. By many accounts, he was the bestselling novelist in China, and his works were widely read in South Korea, Taiwan, and across Southeast Asia. His novels were adapted into films and television series in Japan, South Korea, China, France, and India, with nearly 20 screen adaptations to his name.

Titles including Journey Under the Midnight Sun, The Miracles of the Namiya General Store, and The Camphorwood Custodian found audiences well beyond the mystery genre. His most recent anime film adaptation, The Camphorwood Custodian, opened in Japanese theatres in January 2026 and screened at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival in June.

A Legacy of Quiet Influence

Higashino served as the 13th president of the Mystery Writers of Japan from 2009 to 2013 and later joined the selection committee for the Naoki Prize. Following the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake, he donated royalties from 100,000 reprinted copies of The Wings of the Kirin to relief efforts. In 2023, he received Japan's Medal with Purple Ribbon for his contributions to literature.

Despite his stature, Higashino was known for avoiding public attention. In a 2011 interview, he said he simply wanted his readers to be "continually surprised" by his ideas — a goal that shaped four decades of relentless output. His 106th and final published work, a new Galileo series installment, is scheduled for release on August 5.

For readers across Asia — including the large Indian diaspora community in Japan and the growing number of Indian fans who discovered his work through translations and Bollywood adaptations — Higashino's death marks the loss of a writer who proved that crime fiction could be both intellectually rigorous and deeply humane.
